2026's 11 Most Scenic Queensland Towns

Just outside Yungaburra, hundreds of aerial roots hang in a curtain around the massive trunk of the Curtain Fig Tree, and that is only one of the scenic surprises waiting in Queensland's smaller towns. Near Montville, the Kondalilla Falls circuit leads you through subtropical rainforest to a waterfall dropping into the valley below. Stanthorpe makes a convenient base for Girraween National Park, where you can take in the Pyramid and other granite formations among massive boulders and eucalyptus forest. Farther north, Flagstaff Hill in Port Douglas looks out over Four Mile Beach, the Coral Sea, and the surrounding mountains. Read on to discover the most scenic towns to explore in Queensland this year.

Queensland Towns Made For A Weekend AwayThese Queensland towns make easy, rewarding weekend escapes.

Montville

Perched high in Queensland's Sunshine Coast Hinterland, Montville features lush mountain scenery along with a charming village atmosphere. The town's main street is lined with historic architecture, boutique shops, and a variety of cafés, galleries, and restaurants, making it easy to spend a leisurely morning exploring before heading into the surrounding rainforest. Visitors can browse the Montville Art Gallery which features a collection of original art from throughout the region, pick up handmade sweets from the fun selection at Fudgyboombahs, or stop at the distinctive Clock Shop to view their collection of whimsical clocks and other home goods. The village's elevated position also provides gorgeous views across the green hinterland toward the coast.

The scenery becomes even more dramatic at nearby Kondalilla National Park, where the Kondalilla Falls circuit winds through subtropical rainforest to a majestic waterfall dropping into the valley below. The park also offers shorter walking options for travelers who want to enjoy the rainforest without committing to the longer circuit. With boutique accommodations, rainforest retreats, and plenty of places to grab a bite, Montville easily transforms a scenic outing into a relaxing hinterland getaway.

Maleny

Rolling green hills, dairy farms, dense rainforest, and views of the distinctive Glass House Mountains give Maleny some of the most recognizable scenery in the Sunshine Coast Hinterland. The small town is also known for its creative and food-focused character, with galleries, cafés, local cheese and dairy producers, and independent shops adding plenty to do between scenic outings. Maleny Botanic Gardens & Bird World is particularly worthwhile for its flourishing gardens, expansive views across the surrounding countryside, and assortment of exotic birds and plants.

For a deeper immersion into the region's natural beauty, Mary Cairncross Scenic Reserve protects 55 hectares of subtropical rainforest overlooking the Glass House Mountains and includes scenic walking trails and a Discovery Centre. The spectacular Gardners Falls provides another popular outdoor stop, with a creek, swimming holes, and forested surroundings. Back in town, Maleny's assortment of art galleries, such as The Joy Collective, along with local food producers create an interesting balance between the scenery and the region's creative and agrarian culture.

Stanthorpe

At the heart of Queensland's Granite Belt, Stanthorpe offers a very different landscape from the state's tropical north. Vineyards, orchards, rolling countryside, and enormous granite formations surround this elevated inland town, creating a stunning setting that changes noticeably with the seasons. The region is particularly appealing to travelers interested in food and wine, with popular cellar doors such as Ridgemill Estate, farm shops, cafés, restaurants, and locally produced cheeses and preserves at spots like Blue Pot Pantry & Cafe in nearby Thorndale, providing plenty of reasons to explore beyond the main street.

Stanthorpe is also a convenient base for discovering the wonders of Girraween National Park, where massive granite boulders, a eucalyptus forest, and open valleys create one of southern Queensland's most distinctive landscapes. The park's Pyramid and other granite formations provide memorable viewpoints for hikers and photographers. While the Granite Belt Wine Country offers an easy way to follow a scenic drive between local vineyards and cellar doors.

Yungaburra

Set among the volcanic landscapes and rainforest of the Atherton Tablelands, Yungaburra is one of Queensland's most atmospheric small towns. Its heritage-listed village center is filled with traditional timber buildings, cafés, galleries, restaurants, and the historic Lake Eacham Hotel. While the nearby Peterson Creek provides an opportunity to look for platypuses and other wildlife along the water. The village's old-fashioned streetscape is especially appealing against the surrounding green hills and rainforest.

Just outside town, the enormous Curtain Fig Tree is one of the Tablelands' most unusual natural sights, with hundreds of aerial roots forming a dramatic curtain around its massive trunk. Lake Eacham, a clear volcanic crater lake surrounded by rainforest, is also close by and is popular for swimming, walking, and picnicking. Visitors with more time can continue to Lake Barrine for a rainforest-fringed lake cruise or follow the area's waterfall routes for more stunning sights.

Tamborine Mountain

Rising above the Gold Coast hinterland, Tamborine Mountain is a charming mountain community surrounded by rainforest, waterfalls, walking trails, and sweeping views across southeastern Queensland. Tamborine National Park is the centerpiece, with several sections offering short walks through subtropical rainforest and access to striking waterfalls such as Curtis Falls. The Tamborine Rainforest Skywalk provides another perspective, leading visitors along elevated pathways through the forest canopy and across bridges overlooking the valley.

There is plenty to do when visitors return to town as well. Gallery Walk, the local shopping district, is packed with boutiques, art galleries, cafés, and specialty shops, while the surrounding mountain roads lead to picturesque viewpoints and the beautiful Tamborine Mountain Regional Botanic Gardens. Travelers looking for more active experiences can visit Thunderbird Park for outdoor fun such as a ropes course, zipline tours, and mini golf, or explore the area's wineries and local food producers.

Kuranda

Surrounded by the ancient rainforest of Far North Queensland, Kuranda is one of the state's most distinctive villages. The town sits within the Wet Tropics landscape and is known for its markets, galleries, local shops, and rainforest atmosphere, but the journey into and around Kuranda is just as memorable as the village itself. The Kuranda Scenic Railway winds through Barron Gorge, while the Skyrail Rainforest Cableway offers a bird's-eye view over the forest canopy.

Barron Falls is the area's defining natural attraction, with an elevated lookout providing views across the gorge and cascading waterfall. Visitors can also explore rainforest boardwalks at the Skyrail's Red Peak and Barron Falls stations, or wander through the village's markets and arts scene, such as the Kuranda Arts Co-op. With verdant green rainforest seemingly surrounding every part of town, Kuranda offers an unusually immersive way to experience Queensland's tropical landscape.

Queensland Towns Where Time Slows DownThese Queensland towns preserve the character of earlier eras.

Cooktown

Where the Endeavour River meets the tropical landscapes of Cape York, Cooktown combines rugged scenery with a fascinating historical setting. The town's wide streets and antique buildings reflect its 19th-century past, while the surrounding mountains, rainforest, river, and coast give it a much wilder backdrop than many historic Queensland towns. The Cooktown Botanic Gardens are a natural and cultural highlight, covering 62 hectares of tropical plant life and including the Vera Scarth-Johnson Gallery.

For panoramic views, the climb to Grassy Hill Lookout is difficult to beat, particularly around sunrise or sunset when the Endeavour River and surrounding coastline catch the changing light. Mount Cook National Park provides additional opportunities for bushwalking and views across the Endeavour Valley toward the coast. Visitors can also explore the Cooktown Museum and Reconciliation Rocks to learn more about the area's European and Indigenous history.

Port Douglas

Port Douglas may be better known as a tropical resort destination, but its relatively small population and spectacular natural setting give it a strong claim among Queensland's most scenic towns. Palm-lined Four Mile Beach stretches along the eastern edge of the peninsula, with the cerulean Coral Sea on one side and rainforest-covered mountains on the other. The beach is ideal for a morning walk or a sunset stroll, while the nearby town center adds restaurants, cafés, boutiques, galleries, and marina-side dining at restaurants like Melaleuca to the experience.

Flagstaff Hill provides one of the area's best viewpoints, looking over Four Mile Beach, the Coral Sea, and the surrounding mountains. Visitors can also walk along Dickson Inlet or use Port Douglas as a base for trips to the Great Barrier Reef and nearby Daintree landscapes. The pairing of tropical beaches, lush mountains, warm waters, and a lively village center makes Port Douglas particularly photoworthy throughout the year.

Airlie Beach

Airlie Beach is the mainland gateway to the Whitsundays, but the town itself is idyllic enough to deserve more than a quick stop before heading to the islands. Lush hills descend toward the Coral Sea, with boats scattered across the water and the Whitsunday Islands visible offshore. The Bicentennial Walkway follows the waterfront, while the Airlie Beach Lagoon provides a popular place to swim and relax close to the center of town.

The town also offers a more energetic side, with waterfront restaurants, cute cafés, boutiques, markets, and operators running sailing, snorkeling, reef, and island excursions. Day trips to Whitehaven Beach and the Great Barrier Reef reveal some of the region's most spectacular scenery, while exciting helicopter rides provide a different perspective on the turquoise water and nearby islands.

Noosa Heads

Surrounded by beaches, rainforest, extensive waterways, and the Noosa National Park, Noosa Heads has a picture perfect setting that manages to blend natural beauty with a polished coastal village atmosphere. Noosa Main Beach is the town's centerpiece, with calm waters and a broad sandy shoreline backed by the restaurants, cafés, boutiques, and resorts of Hastings Street. A walk along the coastal track through Noosa National Park adds cliffs, forest, secluded beaches, and ocean viewpoints to the itinerary, with the possibility of spotting interesting wildlife along the way.

Noosa Spit offers another beautiful place to watch the sun set where the river meets the sea, while the surrounding waterways provide ample opportunities for kayaking, paddleboarding, boating, and waterfront dining. Hastings Street also makes Noosa Heads especially appealing for travelers who want beautiful scenery without sacrificing shopping and delicious dining.

Agnes Water

With a long sandy beach, coastal bushland, and easy access to the waters around the Discovery Coast, Agnes Water offers a quieter interpretation of Queensland's tropical coastline. Agnes Water Beach is the town's main draw, providing opportunities for swimming, surfing, walking the shoreline, and watching the changing colors of the Coral Sea. Nearby, the historic Town of 1770 sits around a sheltered coastal inlet and provides the perfect setting for kayaking, paddleboarding, boating, and sunset excursions.

Travelers can also explore the surrounding national parks and coastal landscapes, while local operators offer four-wheel-drive tours, scenic flights, diving, snorkeling, and other exciting ways to experience the coast. The area's small-town atmosphere is complemented by cozy cafés, restaurants, and top-notch accommodations, such as 1770 Getaway and the Agnes Water Beach Club, making it comfortable to stay several days rather than simply passing through.

Queensland Towns With Unforgettable Main StreetsThese main streets showcase Queensland's unique blend of coastal beauty, history, and culture.

See What These Beautiful Queensland Towns Have To Offer

Queensland's scenic towns reveal just how varied the state's landscapes can be. Montville and Maleny showcase the lush hills and rainforest of the Sunshine Coast Hinterland, while Stanthorpe brings vineyards, orchards, and granite formations to the table. Yungaburra and Kuranda immerse visitors in the tropical landscapes of the Atherton Tablelands and Wet Tropics, and Cooktown blends coastal wilderness with a rich historical setting. Tamborine Mountain adds waterfalls and rainforest to the Gold Coast hinterland, while Port Douglas and Airlie Beach provide two very different ways to experience Queensland's tropical coast. Noosa Heads pairs beaches and national park scenery with a lively village atmosphere, and Agnes Water offers a slower-paced coastal escape. Whether the goal is to hike through tropical rainforest, admire soaring mountain views, explore a historic main street, or simply sit and relax by the water, these small Queensland towns prove that some of the state's most beautiful experiences can be found well beyond its major cities.
